passage:
The dhol at Dilnaz's wedding was so loud that Nazia and Imran had to sit on the back steps of the hall, knees touching, to hear each other. They had twenty minutes before the family photo.
"Everyone keeps asking when ours is," Imran said. "So let's not do the vague version. Where would we live?"
"Hyderabad, near my job, for at least three years."
"Ammi wants us in Lucknow. I'll tell her we're deciding that, not her."
"Children?"
"One, maybe, later," he said. "You?"
"Two. But I can live with maybe for now, if we talk again next year."
"And if I get the posting abroad?"
"Then we look at it together. My father will need someone near him when he retires, too."
"Then we plan for that as well."
Someone shouted their names for the photo. They stood up, not fully agreed on children, but clearer than any "don't worry, it'll work out" had ever made them.

qa.q: How long did Nazia and Imran have before the family photo?
qa.a: They had twenty minutes before the family photo.

qa.q: What does Imran's wish to skip 'the vague version' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems tired of vague answers and hopeful that concrete talk now will leave them feeling more secure than easy reassurance ever did.

qa.q: Why is this concrete talk a useful turning point before a wedding?
qa.a: They discover a real difference about children while they can still plan around it and revisit it, which costs far less than finding it after marrying.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel hearing Imran say he'll tell his Ammi that they are deciding?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and respected, because it shows he will stand with her rather than let his mother choose their city.

grounding: Shows a couple replacing vague reassurance with concrete talk about where to live, children, careers and parents before marrying.

subtype: Stage 6: Choosing each other, with eyes open [Response]
passage:
Jomon: Reached home?
Anirban: Just now. Still thinking about what you said at dinner 🙂
Jomon: That I leave wet towels on the bed and you plan holidays till they stop being fun?
Anirban: That part too 😅
Anirban: No, the other part. That when we fought about my night shifts in March, we sat on the kitchen floor and talked till 2 am and nobody walked out.
Jomon: That's the part I trust most. Not the fireworks. The floor.
Anirban: I used to think love had to feel like the first month. It doesn't. It feels like this.
Jomon: Like a cold kitchen floor?
Anirban: Like knowing how we fix things.
Anirban: So yes. Let's tell both our families on Sunday. I'm choosing you, towels included.
Jomon: Choosing you too. Spreadsheet holidays and all ❤️

qa.q: What did Anirban and Jomon do when they fought about the night shifts in March?
qa.a: They sat on the kitchen floor and talked till 2 am, and nobody walked out.

qa.q: What does Anirban's line 'It feels like this' suggest about Anirban's feelings?
qa.a: Anirban feels calm and secure rather than dazzled, trusting the way they fix things more than the excitement of the first month.

qa.q: Which choice makes this commitment likely to hold, and why?
qa.a: They choose each other while naming real flaws, like wet towels and over-planned holidays, and they trust a way of repairing fights they have already tested.

qa.q: If Jomon had hidden the annoyance about the holidays, what might change?
qa.a: Anirban would be committing to an edited version of Jomon, and the unspoken irritation could surface later instead of being known and accepted now.

grounding: Shows a couple committing with full knowledge of each other's flaws and trust in the way they resolve trouble.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage: Ankita, you think your Leela Nani was always sensible? At sixteen I was not. There was a boy on the next terrace, Shekhar, and every evening once the streetlights came on we talked across the wall. Hours, beta. About the stars, his cricket, my cousin's wedding, nothing and everything. I hurried through dinner to get back up there. My friend Sunita waited for me at the badminton court for a week, then stopped waiting. My algebra book stayed shut under my pillow. When Shekhar went to his aunt's for a week, the whole world felt switched off, and I sat on the terrace anyway, just in case. My mother asked why I no longer laughed at the dinner table. I could not have told her. It felt as if the only real thing left in the world was that wall.

qa.q: Where did Leela and Shekhar talk every evening?
qa.a: They talked across the wall between their terraces every evening once the streetlights came on.

qa.q: How did the young Leela feel when Shekhar went away to his aunt's?
qa.a: She felt empty and lost, as if the whole world had been switched off, so she sat on the terrace anyway, just in case.

qa.q: When Sunita stopped waiting at the badminton court, what could the young Leela have done?
qa.a: She could have taken it as a warning, gone to Sunita, and kept some evenings for friends and algebra so Shekhar was not her whole world.

qa.q: What might Sunita have been experiencing that week at the badminton court?
qa.a: Sunita probably felt hurt and left out, waiting evening after evening and then giving up when her friend kept choosing the terrace.

grounding: Shows a first teenage romance so consuming that friendships and studies quietly fade into the background.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Phone hour in the girls' hostel ran from eight to nine, and Farida's phone buzzed at 8:01. Nikhil: "Hey?" At 8:03: "You there?" At 8:04: "Busy? 😕" She turned it face down and opened her chemistry notes. Across the room Irawati raised an eyebrow. "Not replying?"
"In a bit," Farida said, and did not move.
A month ago she had waited by the charging point for his first message. Now each buzz felt like a tap on her shoulder that would not stop. At 8:40 she typed "sorry, studying" and deleted the longer line under it: "can we not talk every single minute?"
His reply came in three seconds: "ok. you've been busy a lot lately."
She stared at the word lately for a while. Then she wrote, "haha no, just exams 🙂" and switched off the screen, and neither of them said what they meant.

qa.q: When did phone hour run in the girls' hostel?
qa.a: Phone hour ran from eight to nine.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as Nikhil's messages kept coming?
qa.a: She felt irritated and crowded, as if each buzz were a tap on her shoulder that would not stop, though she hid it behind short replies.

qa.q: What small, honest step could Farida take at this stage instead of 'haha no, just exams'?
qa.a: She could say kindly that she likes talking but needs quiet during study time, so the crack is named while it is still small.

qa.q: How might Nikhil be reading Farida's short replies?
qa.a: Nikhil seems to sense her growing distance, since he says she's been busy a lot lately, and he may feel hurt or worried and message more because of it.

grounding: Shows small cracks in a teen relationship, with one irritated by constant contact, the other sensing distance, and neither saying so.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
After tuition, Jagdish walked slower than usual so that Sonal would reach the bus stop first. She didn't; she waited for him under the neem tree.
"You didn't call last night," she said.
"Tired," he said, which was partly true. What he couldn't say was that their nightly calls had started to feel like homework he had never chosen. On Saturday he had hinted, "Maybe we both need more time with friends?" and she had laughed and texted him twice as often.
Now she held out a keychain she had made with his initials. "For your bag."
He took it, said "Nice," and felt worse.
His friend Omkar, who had watched from the tea stall, asked later, "Are you two okay?"
Jagdish shrugged. "She's too much these days."
Omkar looked at him for a moment. "Or are you just not saying something?"

qa.q: What did Sonal give Jagdish at the bus stop?
qa.a: She gave him a keychain she had made with his initials, for his bag.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he took the keychain and said 'Nice'?
qa.a: He felt guilty and trapped, because the calls had come to feel like unchosen homework, yet he could not bring himself to say so.

qa.q: What could help break this cycle of hints and clinging?
qa.a: Jagdish could say plainly and kindly what he feels instead of hinting about more time with friends, so Sonal is not left guessing and holding on harder.

qa.q: What is it like for Sonal when Jagdish goes quiet and slow?
qa.a: Sonal senses a change without knowing what it is, so she waits, asks about the missed call and makes him a gift, trying to hold on.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels bored and trapped hinting instead of speaking, while the partner senses a change and becomes clingier.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Ines had decided on Sunday, walking her dog along the river in Seville: it was over with Jin. She just hadn't told him.
On Monday he saved her a seat in the canteen, as always. On Tuesday he sent a photo of two tickets for the school film night on Friday, with a heart. "Great!" she typed, and disliked herself a little. Her friends would talk; his friends would take sides; and his face, when she said it, would be the worst part. Maybe after the film night. Maybe after exams.
On Thursday, by the lockers, Jin said, "You seem far away. Is it me?"
"No, just tired," she said. She watched his shoulders relax, and felt the lie settle on her, heavier than the truth would have been.

qa.q: What did Jin send Ines on Tuesday?
qa.a: He sent a photo of two tickets for the school film night on Friday, with a heart.

qa.q: Why does Ines keep putting off telling Jin?
qa.a: She is afraid of hurting Jin and dreads the fuss among their friends, so delay feels kinder, though she feels guilty each time she pretends.

qa.q: What turning point does Ines have on Thursday, and what could she do with it?
qa.a: When Jin asks if it is him, she could answer honestly and kindly, in private, instead of saying she's tired and letting him hope longer.

qa.q: How is the delay affecting Jin right now?
qa.a: Jin keeps hoping, saving her seat and buying tickets, and relaxes at her answer, so the ending, when it comes, may hurt him more.

grounding: Shows a teen who has privately decided to end a relationship delaying out of fear of hurting the other, while the other keeps hoping.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
I was on the other bed pretending to do my maths when Didi called Ritu. I'm not sure what Damini was feeling; her hand kept smoothing the bedsheet flat. She didn't text it, which I thought she would. She said, "Ritu, I need to tell you something properly. I don't feel the same any more, and I don't want to mislead you."
There was a long quiet on the other end. Didi didn't say "maybe later" or "it's not you, it's me", or anything about Ritu being clingy, which she had grumbled to me about before. She just said, "You were good to me. I'm sorry this hurts." Then she listened.
After the call she sat with her face in her hands. I brought her a glass of water. She said, "That was the hardest ten minutes of my life," and I believed her.

qa.q: What was the narrator pretending to do during the call?
qa.a: The narrator was on the other bed pretending to do maths.

qa.q: What might the narrator have been feeling while watching Damini make the call?
qa.a: The narrator seems tense and protective, noticing her hand smoothing the sheet, and caring enough to bring water afterwards.

qa.q: Which parts of Damini's call made the ending clear and kind?
qa.a: She called instead of texting, said plainly that she didn't feel the same, left out excuses, blame and 'maybe later', and then listened.

qa.q: What is Ritu likely experiencing on the other end of the call?
qa.a: Ritu is probably hurt and stunned, hence the long quiet, but is spared false hope and insults, which may make healing easier later.

grounding: Shows a teen ending a relationship by phone, briefly and honestly, without blame or false hope, as seen by a younger sibling.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Dear Sudha Didi,
You said to write when it felt too big for the phone, so here it is. Manav ended things on Friday. He was kind about it, which somehow makes it worse.
Since then my chest feels hollow, like someone scooped it out. I keep opening his profile to see if he's posted, if he looks happy, who liked what. Forty times yesterday, maybe.
Last night I typed a caption about "people who pretend to care" and my thumb was on Post. Then I remembered you saying, "Don't write anything at midnight that you'd hate at noon," and I deleted it.
Today Meenal came over with samosas and we watched a silly film, and for two whole hours I forgot. Amma hugged me without asking anything.
Tell me honestly: does it really get smaller?
Your Aparna

qa.q: When did Manav end things?
qa.a: Manav ended things on Friday.

qa.q: What is Aparna feeling since Friday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aparna feels hurt and hollow, describing a scooped-out chest and checking Manav's profile about forty times in one day.

qa.q: What helped Aparna at this stage, and what could keep helping?
qa.a: Deleting the midnight caption and spending time with Meenal and Amma helped; leaning on people like that, and checking the profile less, lets the pain ease.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sudha may feel moved, and glad that the midnight advice stopped the post, and will likely want to reassure Aparna that the pain does get smaller 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager who was left feeling rejected and hollow, resisting a spiteful post and leaning on friends and family.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Sunday, 11 p.m.
Five years with Bhupen this winter. Tonight was the usual: khichdi, the cooking show, him on the left of the sofa, me on the right, both scrolling. At ten he said, "Chai, Leela-ji?" in that mock-formal voice, and I said yes without looking up.
It's easy. I love easy.
But today I noticed new running shoes by the door, and I don't know when he started running, or why. And I haven't told him I've been looking at an evening design course; the form has sat open on my laptop for three weeks.
When did we stop asking each other things? We know each other's chai sugar to the grain, and not what the other thinks about on the bus.
Maybe tomorrow I'll ask about the shoes.

qa.q: What did Leela notice by the door today?
qa.a: Leela noticed new running shoes by the door.

qa.q: What does the question 'When did we stop asking each other things?' show about how Leela feels?
qa.a: Leela feels content in the easy routine yet uneasy and a little lonely, noticing that neither knows what the other is quietly thinking about.

qa.q: What small step could help at this comfortable stage?
qa.a: Asking Bhupen about the running and mentioning the design course over chai would reopen curiosity before more small changes go unspoken.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be experiencing in these easy evenings?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel comfortable but unasked, having started running without it ever coming up, perhaps assuming nobody is curious.

grounding: Shows a couple of several years in an easy routine where comfort has quietly replaced curiosity, so small changes go unspoken.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage: You asked why I never took the Singapore job, Maria. Sit, your tea will go cold. At twenty-five, I, Rukmini, the eager young engineer, had an offer there. Anand, whom I was seeing then, had just bought a scooter to take his parents to the temple every Friday in Kochi. He wanted our life right there, near his mother's garden. I wanted the airport. We both knew it. Yet our talks became very polite. "How was work?" "Fine. Yours?" When the offer letter came, I left it in my drawer and said, "Let's discuss after Onam." After Onam, he said, "After my sister's exam." We kept pushing the big question to later, like a box nobody wanted to open. That box does not get lighter with waiting, Maria. It only gets heavier.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini have a job offer?
qa.a: Rukmini had a job offer in Singapore.

qa.q: What was the young Rukmini feeling when she left the offer letter in her drawer?
qa.a: She felt torn and uneasy, wanting the airport yet afraid of what saying so would do to her and Anand, so she hid behind 'after Onam'.

qa.q: When the offer letter arrived, what could the young Rukmini have done instead of postponing?
qa.a: She could have shown Anand the letter and asked plainly how each of them saw the future, even if the answer was hard to hear.

qa.q: What might Anand have been experiencing as their talks grew polite and short?
qa.a: Anand probably sensed the distance too, since he also pushed the question to after his sister's exam, perhaps fearing what an honest talk would reveal.

grounding: Shows a young couple pulled apart by a career move and a wish to stay near family, with talks about the future turning polite and postponed.
